findings.title: GhostShares 2: Grok Apps Exposed xAI's Business Secrets and People's Private Data (Claroc Research)
findings.summary_md: Claroc Research, authored by Asaf Aprozper, published the primary research on November 10, 2026, three hours and twenty-seven minutes before this story's first_seen. The team resolved 43,601 names under grok.me by subdomain discovery, opened the first page of 43,551 addresses from the public internet while signed in to nothing, found 37,571 still online and 35,578 of those (94.7 percent) opening for anyone; only 1,993 answered HTTP 401. The post dates the start of the work to November 8, 2026, the SpaceXSI security.txt notification to that same afternoon, the report of the remaining 22 staff apps to November 9, and the vendor reply to November 10. It also documents the Grok Build publish panel offering Anyone with the link preselected, a team app whose generated sign-in logic let an uninvited Google account read, edit and delete records, and an estimate of roughly 650 to 800 apps holding private data.

findings.title: GhostShares: A Shared Muse Chat Exposed Prep for a Confidential Call With a Frontier AI Lab Leader (Claroc Research, GhostShares 1)
findings.summary_md: Three weeks before the Grok Build findings, the same team published the first GhostShares report on Meta's Muse assistant, which publishes shared conversations as pages that open for anyone holding the link. The post explains the technique the Grok research later reused: Muse named each share's address after the conversation title, passive DNS and subdomain discovery listed those hostnames, and an incognito session with no login returned personal files and internal company documents. On October 20, 2026, after Ars Technica asked about the findings, Meta told the outlet it was suspending the feature; Claroc rechecked 40 shares that day and none opened, though the hostnames and titles remained in passive DNS history. The Grok Build post cites this earlier work directly and applies the same findability argument to every published AI app that gets its own hostname.

findings.title: Railway security incident: finding the apps your employees deployed (Claroc Research)
findings.summary_md: Published October 22, 2026 and updated October 26, this Claroc post predates the Grok Build research and covers the platform-side version of the same problem: environment variables holding AI provider keys, payment keys, database passwords and cloud credentials sitting in a hosted build platform. The post records the revocation request Railway's status page linked at 21:48 UTC on October 21, 2026, and shows the method Claroc later reused for AI-built apps, which is enumerating what a company's employees deployed outside IT's view. It is relevant background rather than part of the Grok Build disclosure, since the Grok research does not cite it.

findings.title: LinkDrift: How Leaked Links Exposed Internal Files at Fortune 500 Companies (Claroc Research)
findings.summary_md: Claroc's October 5, 2026 LinkDrift report established the access-control pattern the Grok Build research extends: share links already circulating in malware logs and public indexes still opened corporate material with no exploit and no login. The dataset covered 326 organizations, with about 800 accessible links among Fortune 500 companies and sensitive or internal material confirmed at 19 of them; one link exposed a folder reporting 8,496 files and 749.1 GB. The Grok Build post does not cite LinkDrift, but both rest on the finding that an unguessable URL handed out as an access control keeps working for anyone who obtains it.
